drills.q: State the difference between a citation that exists and a citation that supports the claim, with one number.
drills.a: Existence is plausibility (resolves, right domain, on topic); support is faithfulness (the cited span entails the sentence). The 2026 deep-research audit measured link-works at 94-100% and topical relevance at 80-96% while fact-check accuracy ran 24-77%.

drills.q: Write out ALCE citation recall and precision.
drills.a: Recall(s) = 1 if the concatenation of s's cited docs entails s. Precision(d) = 1 if d alone entails s, or if removing d from the cited set breaks entailment. Report mean recall over sentences, mean precision over citations, and unsupported-sentence rate = 1 − mean recall.

drills.q: Why does a dense retriever hand you the chunk that states the opposite?
drills.a: Because it scores semantic similarity, not entailment, and negation barely moves an embedding. The chunk most similar to a claim is often the one discussing the same topic while asserting the contrary. This is the core reason relevance is not support.

drills.q: Name the architectural property that makes post-hoc citation unfixable by prompting.
drills.a: There is no reachable output meaning 'nothing supports this'. The answer precedes the search, so retrieval is confirmatory, and the instruction makes a citation mandatory. Abstention has to be a live branch in the pipeline, not a phrase you hope the model chooses.

drills.q: Your NLI verifier flags 40% of sentences as unsupported and the answers look fine. Debug in order.
drills.a: 1) Decontextualisation — flagged sentences starting with pronouns give neutral verdicts. 2) Premise length — 1,200-token premises drift to neutral; split into 3-sentence windows and max-pool. 3) Threshold — 0.5 is not universal; label ~200 pairs from your corpus and fit tau. 4) Granularity — a two-claim sentence with one supported claim correctly fails; decompose. 5) Only then, it may really be 40%.

drills.q: Attribute-first versus generate-then-verify: pick one and justify the sequence.
drills.a: Generate-then-verify first, because it is a bolt-on that immediately gives you the measurement (unsupported rate, recall, precision) and you cannot manage what you cannot measure. Then attribute-first, because verification only detects and does not raise the ceiling. Costs are opposite: verification adds latency and can only reject; attribute-first adds a pass, lowers fluency, lowers coverage.

drills.q: Why does deep-research citation accuracy fall as search depth rises? Give the numbers.
drills.a: Attention dilution during synthesis. GPT-5.4 fact-check accuracy fell 79% at 2 tool calls to 17% at 150, while link validity and relevance stayed above 92%. The models producing the most citations had the lowest fact-check accuracy, so selective citation beats exhaustive citation.

drills.q: A citation entails the claim and the answer is still wrong. Give two mechanisms and their fixes.
drills.a: Supersession — v1.4 entails it but v2.1 overrides; fix with effective_from / superseded_by metadata filtered at retrieval and retire old docs from the index. Cherry-picking — the cited span is the exception clause; fix with a contradiction sweep across the other retrieved chunks and surface the conflict instead of picking a side.

drills.q: Design the verification stage for a 20-sentence answer over 8 retrieved chunks. Give the cost.
drills.a: Decontextualise per response (1 small call), split each chunk into overlapping 3-sentence windows, build all (window, sentence) pairs and score in ONE batched forward pass with MiniCheck or HHEM-2.1-open, max-pool per sentence per doc. Roughly 20-60 pairs plus union and leave-one-out pairs for precision. Batched on GPU: tens of milliseconds. Unbatched over HTTP: hundreds. Batching is not optional.

drills.q: Does RAG solve hallucination? One sentence with the study.
drills.a: No — Stanford RegLab measured commercial legal RAG products at 17-33% hallucination versus 43% for GPT-4, a real reduction and nowhere near the '100% hallucination-free' being marketed.

drills.q: Why is a verbatim quote check the first thing you build, despite being trivial?
drills.a: It is free, deterministic, and it catches paraphrased-quote fabrication which NLI passes because the paraphrase captures the gist. A fabricated quote fails a human's eyes immediately and passes entailment, so a cheap exact check covers a gap the expensive probabilistic check leaves open.

drills.q: Verify citations for a browsing agent. What are the three non-obvious requirements?
drills.a: 1) Snapshot at fetch time with a content hash and verify against the snapshot, so verification is reproducible and a page edit cannot silently invalidate the audit. 2) Cite snapshot id + URL + timestamp, because 'the page said this on date X' is the only supportable claim. 3) Verify per section during synthesis, not once at the end, since accuracy degrades with search depth.

drills.q: When is showing citations the wrong choice?
drills.a: Single-source assistants (highlight the span instead), creative or synthesis-heavy output (section-level provenance plus on-demand sources), claims drawn from general knowledge with no source being asserted (mark unsourced), and anywhere you cannot verify, since an unverified citation is a false trust signal.

drills.q: Rank attribution interventions by effect per unit of effort.
drills.a: 1) Verbatim quote check. 2) Citation-constrained decoding over in-context ids. 3) Sentence-level entailment gate with abstention. 4) Span-level locators for one-click checking. 5) Corpus supersession metadata. 6) Attribute-first generation. 7) Claim-level atomic decomposition for the high-stakes surface. Dead last: prompting the model to cite more carefully.

drills.q: Why is your internal citation-precision of 0.94 not a comparable number?
drills.a: Automatic attribution metrics have been shown not to transfer across datasets and constructs (arXiv:2606.23915), so the figure tracks your own regressions only. Anchor it with a human audit of ~100 sentences per release before quoting it to anyone.
